01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
eligibility criteria
Requirements a person must meet to qualify.
concede
To admit that something is true.
masthead
The printed name and identifying details of a newspaper.
administrative record
A document made in the course of managing an organisation.
contemporaneous
Existing or recorded at the time an event occurred.
vindicate
To show that a claim or suspicion was justified.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The correction had offered Emma an apparently straightforward task: identify the inaccurate figure in the original report and establish what should have stood in its place. At the library, the first half proved easy. The second did not.

A bound volume of the local newspaper yielded an article dated 16 September 2011, two days before Emma interviewed Claire Morrison. Beneath the headline “Eight Students Chosen for Travel Support,” Malcolm Vale was quoted celebrating the Glenarraidh Education Trust's commitment to widening educational opportunities. Eight applicants, the article asserted, had been selected for travel assistance. It named none of them and described neither the eligibility criteria nor the panel responsible for the decision.

The later correction conceded that the number had been wrong. It supplied no substitute and attributed the error to no one. Emma resisted reading that silence as an admission by the trust: the notice was issued by a newspaper, and its omissions established remarkably little about the organisation's underlying records.

She photographed both pages intact, including the masthead and publication dates. A crop of the disputed sentence might be persuasive on a screen; it could also disguise the difference between a reporter's account and a primary administrative record. Emma wanted to preserve precisely that distinction.

Sarah answered on the third ring. “So the announcement was inflated?”

“We don't know whether it was inflated. We know the paper later corrected its figure. The trust might have supplied the number, the journalist might have misheard it, or the circumstances might have changed before publication. None of those explanations is established.”

Further searching produced a letter from a reader, published shortly afterwards under the heading “Questions About Student Grants.” The writer was identified only as a parent from Glenarraidh and complained that families had not been told how candidates were chosen. The editor had withheld the name. Emma could neither contact the writer from the printed record nor assess whether the complaint came from direct experience. Nevertheless, its contemporary date mattered: uncertainty about the selection procedure had been voiced publicly in 2011.

She constructed a source table. The announcement represented a published claim. The correction documented an acknowledged reporting error. The letter registered a complaint whose factual basis remained unknown. Treating the three as interchangeable would manufacture a certainty that no single document possessed.

In her notes from 18 September, Claire had questioned whether the trust gave students what they had been promised. Emma remembered how readily she had interpreted that remark as personal hostility towards the directors. The newly recovered material did not vindicate Claire's suspicions, but it supplied a more disciplined way to examine them.

Before leaving, Emma wrote Fiona Bell a separate, neutral request: were the criteria for selecting recipients in 2011 retained, and did the trust hold any contemporaneous record of decisions? She did not refer to the withheld caller's instruction about authorising payments. That allegation would be tested on its own merits, not smuggled into a question about eligibility.

At the exit she checked the dates once more. The first report preceded her interview with Claire. The correction followed Claire's disappearance. Between those printed facts lay a period in which assumptions had hardened into public stories.

For Emma, the urgent question was no longer whether the figure eight concealed a scandal. It was who had been entitled to choose—and whether the surviving records could show how the choice was made.
